ZZZ was not expecting there to be hazardous freight in the can and the paperwork ZZZ1 gave us listed no accessible dangerous goods were on the plane. Cause: Someone put a box in the can without making sure it was properly documented.
ASRSN:2228969.s: ZZZ ground crew discovered an undocumented box of accessible dangerous goods in the first can while unloading the aircraft. The reporter attributed the incident to someone placing the box in the can without ensuring it was properly documented.

ASRSN:2228984.n: 7 miles out on the approach to ZZZ for ILS runway XX, we noticed traffic climbing toward us as we were LEVEL at 2000 feet. It began climbing from 800 feet below us and we received an RA with aural Monitor vertical speed", when it was 500 feet below us and appeared to be still climbing, we disconnected the autopilot, climbed 500 feet to 2500 feet, which was a safe altitude and once traffic passed, descended back to our assigned altitude of 2000 feet. We notified approach of the RA, the climb, and return to assigned altitude, all of which were ignored as Controller seemed task saturated. We continued the approach without incident.Cause: Aircraft climbing under us on approach" I was pilot flying on the approach into ZZZ RWY XX. We were level at 2000 feet MSL about 2 or 3 miles outside of the initial approach fix, ZZZZ. At this time an aircraft was climbing into us (about 800 feet below us, the aircraft climbed to a little less than 500 feet underneath us). We heard the 'traffic' aural and then received an RA, the aural alert said 'monitor vertical speed'. We proceeded to climb to about 2500 MSL when the PM noticed that the aircraft underneath us had leveled off and was no longer a factor. The PM told approach that we were responding to an RA and would continue the approach into RWY XX. The Approach Controller never answered us, so we proceeded to talk to ZZZ Tower to continue the approach. The rest of the flight continued without any issue.Cause: We had been cleared for the approach and an aircraft was starting to climb into us. We were following the altitudes assigned.Suggestions: For Approach to monitor aircraft separation in that area.
ASRSN:2228984.s: The pilot flying an ILS approach to ZZZ RWY XX at 2000 feet received a "monitor vertical speed" RA from a climbing aircraft 500 feet below. The crew climbed to 2500 feet, but the Approach Controller appeared task saturated and ignored their notification before they contacted Tower to continue.

ASRSN:2228987.n: Flying into DCA at night accepted river visual got low and received a GPWS alert went around. Cause: Accepted visual instead of flying RNAV
ASRSN:2228987.s: The pilot flying into DCA at night accepted a River Visual approach, descended too low, and triggered a GPWS alert, resulting in a go-around. The pilot attributed the incident to accepting the visual approach instead of flying the RNAV procedure.

ASRSN:2228999.n: Upon arrival at Gate XX we were informed by our gate agent that our airplane was waiting on maintenance. When we boarded the airplane the PCA (Aircraft Preconditioned Air Unit) was connected but not running so I called Operations for ramp to come over and turn it on. The APU was running providing power, but not air. Already knowing the tail, I radioed local maintenance to see if we could run the bleed air and asked them if they had an ETA the logbook would be ready. I was told that they were waiting to complete the logbook, but there was no ETA when that would be. Not too long after that another mechanic arrived at the plane and I asked him what the issue was and were told that the previous week they had found metal chips in the engine oil and after a subsequent inspection that night they had recovered additional metal fragments from the aft sump, but the inspection procedure they had been operating under did not give any guidance about what to do in the event they found metal in the subsequent inspection. That was what they were waiting for from engineering. The mechanic also showed us a picture of what I believe he said was the first set of fragment they had recovered the previous week. The fragments were laid out on a grid to show their relative size. He said they believe they were from a bearing in the #1 engine based on the studies that had been done on them. After being informed that engineering had approved an additional inspection schedule I formally initiated the procedure I was questioning the safety of the aircraft. I had previously initiating the procedure with my original dispatcher, but at the request of her supervisor we all decided to wait for the engineer's decision before pulling that trigger. I spoke the Chief Pilot where we had a professional discussion about the situation but ultimately decided to wait until I had the logbook so I could review the history of the airplane as best I could. One question I did get from the Chief Pilot was would my decision to refuse the plane change if I hadn't been informed by the local mechanic about the actual condition of the engine." I found this question to be disturbing for obvious reasons. Once the logbook arrived I review the last few pages to find that the plane had been operating on a deferral for the #1 EMCD (Electronic Master Chip Detector) and that deferral had been cleared. It looked as if that was the deferral that was used when the metal fragments were originally discovered. I phoned Maintenance Control to verify and to ask if, since the airplane had required inspections before each takeoff under the original MEL, would continue to be the case. After reviewing his information he said it would not. Moving forward under the new guidance from manual they weren't required to inspect it again for and additional 50-70 flight hours. This didn't appear to add-up since there were 2 known occasions in a matter of 1 week where metal fragments were found in the engine oil . The timeline looked like the #1 EMCD tripped and the corrective action was to defer the #1 EMCD. At some point shortly after metal fragments were recovered and sent in for analyses. Over the course of a few days recurring inspections of the #1 EMCD were conducted and signed-off on. Then on night of Day 0 additional metal fragments were found in the aft sump and the corrective action was to close out the #1 EMCD deferral and put in place a different inspection protocol that didn't have anyone look again for another 50-70 flight hours. This was not adding up since on multiple occasions metal fragments had been found. I again refused the aircraft as the safety of the aircraft was in doubt. As we concluded the conference call between myself, dispatch, and the Chief Pilot one of them told the other to just replace the crew as we ended the call. My observation of the events of this report is that the integrity of the schedule was the number one priority - to the complete exclusion of safety. As the pilot in command, my assessment of the aircraft maintenance history, MEL application, and discussions with maintenance technicians regarding the presence of metal shavings indicated by the chip detector was completely disregarded. I was unable to legally or ethically sign the dispatch release guaranteeing the safe operation of flight - and dispatch's answer was to find someone else who would. The fact that I was actually asked "if you didn't know what you know about the engine history, would that change your decision" is preposterous. In my XX years as an airline pilot, I have never refused an aircraft before. I do not take it lightly. The complete disregard for the checks and balances of safety is extraordinarily troubling."
ASRSN:2228999.s: The Captain refused to depart at the gate due to unresolved metal fragments in the #1 engine oil and questionable maintenance deferrals. Dispatch and the Chief Pilot disregarded the safety concerns and suggested replacing the crew to maintain the schedule.

ASRSN:2229031.n: Operating flight ABCD from ZZZ to ZZZ1 with XX pax and X crew. On the runway (XXR) the radar was showing a full display of yellow and green precipitation on our departure flight path. We had a tilt of approximately 6 to 7 degrees up. There were no reports of severe turbulence from ATC or other aircraft, however, all previous departures were to the northeast. Once airborne and into the clouds we encountered light and moderate turbulence. I continued to hand fly the aircraft and the FO managed the FCU (Flight Control Unit) as we were given a turn to 150. The FO adjusted the radar appropriately as we climbed. The radar began to show small spots of red and magenta in a field of mostly yellow and some green. I hand flew the aircraft to avoid any red or magenta while in the turn to heading 150. Passing 4000 feet the turbulence increased to all moderate chop and turbulence. I noticed the airspeed increasing and adjusted pitch in an attempt of maintaining 250kts. The airspeed was approaching 260kts with vertical speed indicating up to 6000 fpm and an amber indicator. I said that we must be in an updraft to the FO. Shortly after, we encountered a mix of severe and moderate turbulence.I began to have difficulty focusing my eyes on the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and ND (Navigation Display) due to the turbulence so I engaged the autopilot and continued to monitor the PFD and ND as best I could. We briefly encountered turbulence that pushed us down into our seats followed by a feeling of lightness. The severe turbulence encountered was between 5000 and 9000 feet. I delayed the 10000 foot notification until we were out of the precipitation, approximately 12600 feet. Afterwords I called the cabin crew to ask if everyone was ok and advise that we were out of the precipitation and area of greatest turbulence. They advised me that all crew and pax (passengers) were unharmed but scared for a bit. After the encounter I notified our dispatcher and Maintenance Controller of the severe encounter. The reply from dispatch was Maintenance Controller WANTS TO KNOW IF IT WAS SEVERE OR BAD MOD AND WHAT MAKES YOU THINK ITS SEVERE DUE TO THE LARGE INSPECTION REQUIRED. FROM RA". A logbook entry was made for the severe turbulence encounter"
ASRSN:2229031.s: The flight crew encountered severe turbulence between 5,000 and 9,000 feet while climbing through precipitation on departure, causing airspeed fluctuations and difficulty reading displays. Although all passengers and crew remained unharmed, the dispatcher questioned the severity classification due to the extensive inspection required.

ASRSN:2229032.n: On the takeoff roll, just prior to 40 knots, the LEFT ENGINE FAULT EICAS Message appeared, and a low-speed reject was performed as required by company SOP. The message cleared as we exited the runway, so we were not able to see the Message that triggered the EICAS. Maintenance Control was able to recall the Message at the Gate which was: 79 L ENGINE FAULT - OIL FILTER IMPENDING BYPASS. The engine oil temperature was in the normal range for Takeoff and no faults appeared during taxi and throughout the warmup period. The discrepancy was entered into the logbook and deferred by ZZZ Maintenance Control in accordance with MEL procedures.
ASRSN:2229032.s: During takeoff roll below 40 knots, the crew rejected the takeoff after a "LEFT ENGINE FAULT" EICAS message appeared. Maintenance identified the cause as an impending oil filter bypass, which was deferred per MEL procedures after the message cleared.

ASRSN:2229067.n: When the Captain and I boarded the plane the flight attendants let us know there was a burning electrical smell back by door 3L. The Captain spoke with the FAs and then wrote the issue up and called Maintenance. Maintenance personnel came to the aircraft and began investigating. At least one of them said they could smell the odor as well. They investigated but could not find a source. The Captain and I went back to the area and could no longer smell it at door 3L. However, there was a strong odor that irritated my nose and the Captain's eyes around rows 26/27. Maintenance again investigated and switched on and off the packs and recirculation fans. They were unable to determine a source and said the fumes had gone away and that would sign off the discrepancy. The crew was unsatisfied with the answer and the Captain initiated the process to reject the aircraft. While this was happening the Captain and I were sitting in the flight deck with packs off. I felt like I was getting a small headache and just needed some fresh air. I left the flight deck for a few minutes thinking maybe I was smelling something there. I came back a few minutes later and could definitely smell faint fumes. I asked the Captain to leave and come back and to see what he thought. He was also complaining of a slight headache that had started. He left and came back a few minutes later and could smell something as well. So we initiated a new maintenance write-up for the flight deck.New maintenance personnel came out and multiple members of the team were able to detect the smell as well. There was approximately 2 hours of time lapse between us first getting on board the aircraft and the flight deck odors. At this time the Captain had already rejected the aircraft but now had additional symptoms and a few members of the crew (FAs) were complaining of headaches as well. The Captain spoke to medical personnel who determined he was unfit to fly. However, my symptoms had subsided and I was deemed fit to fly. While this was going on the flight was officially cancelled. We were rescheduled to operate a ferry flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 the next morning.
ASRSN:2229067.s: The flight crew and maintenance personnel investigated a burning electrical odor on the aircraft, which caused headaches and eye irritation for the Captain and First Officer. The Captain was declared unfit to fly and the flight was cancelled after maintenance failed to identify the fume source despite multiple inspections.

ASRSN:2229074.n: While intercepting the 4R localizer into BOS we received a bank angle alert. There had been a heavy 777 and an Airbus join the localizer prior to us. During the last turn to join the localizer we felt wake turbulence roll the airplane right. Captain disconnected the autopilot to counteract the roll and that was about the time we got the bank angle alert. We were on speed and path already and outside the FAF so we continued the approach and landed uneventfully. As we were joining LOC for ILS 4R in BOS, we observed a gradual ongoing roll to the right and aural bank angle" alert. We disconnected autopilot and autothrottle and stabilized the airplane. We only exceeded bank by a degree or two when this occurred. We rejoined the approach and landed uneventfully."
ASRSN:2229074.s: The crew encountered wake turbulence from a preceding 777 and Airbus while intercepting the 4R localizer at BOS, causing a right roll and bank angle alert. They disconnected the autopilot to stabilize the aircraft, exceeded bank by only a degree or two, and completed an uneventful landing.

ASRSN:2229082.n: During preflight we received a Planned Dangerous Goods (DG) Summary showing 1 item in Position *OFF. I informed the FO that it looks like the Dangerous Good has been removed and that there is no Dangerous Goods planned to be on the aircraft. I remarked that there is no need to wait for a Final DG Summary and we will not have to send a DG acknowledgment code.FOM states If DG is loaded, do not release the parking brake until the Final DG Summary is received. With only 1 item listed and it showing a position of *OFF, we assumed that no DG was loaded and we could release the parking brake. After pushback and engine start we received a Final DG Summary. Again, it showed 1 item position *OFF and included a Pilot Notification Form (PNF) showing 0 pieces, 0 weight, dry ice. FOM states: a DG PNF for DG that is shown as OFF" will not be printed.We did receive a printed PNF even though DG was shown as *OFF. It seems that we should not have received a PNF because there was no DG loaded. Dispatch confirmed there was no DG on the aircraft. The Final DG Summary and PNF created some confusion. If we receive a Planned DG Summary showing only 1 item with position *OFF, should we wait for the Final DG Summary and PNF and send a report before releasing the parking brake?Per FOM, if no DG is loaded, neither a PNF nor Final DG Summary is required. So I assumed we could release the parking brake and not have to send a report."
ASRSN:2229082.s: The flight crew released the parking brake before receiving a Final Dangerous Goods Summary because a Planned Summary showed one item as *OFF, indicating no cargo. Confusion arose when a printed Pilot Notification Form was received despite Dispatch confirming no dangerous goods were loaded.

ASRSN:2229114.n: We were taxiing into the gate at ORD. As we approached Taxiway CS, we were cleared into the Ramp. Our instructions were to enter the Ramp via CS and then transition to the B taxi lane to the gate. While we were on CS, I saw on my Airport Moving Map (AMM) taxi chart that the B taxi lane diverts early to the right. As we were abeam the turn, I stopped the aircraft for clarification. We asked if we could take the C taxi lane and then transition to B to the gate due to the position of where our gate was located. The Ramp Controller approved our request. We arrived at the gate as scheduled. The reason why I am writing this report is mainly due to the new transition taxi lanes on the Ramp when you enter from the south port. These taxi lane lines can be confusing when having to transition from one taxi lane to the other. There are several transition taxi lines on the ground and they are not clearly marked in how they exactly transition from the entry point to the intended taxi lane. These transition lines are only available on the AMM and not depicted on the 20-9. I have had several occasions where you have to check the AMM multiple times to make sure you are transitioning from the Ramp entry point to the correct taxi lane due to multiple taxi lines going in multiple directions.
ASRSN:2229114.s: The pilot reported confusion while taxiing at ORD due to unclear ground markings for new ramp transition lanes from the south port. Although the crew stopped to clarify and received an approved alternate route to the gate, the reporter noted these complex transitions are only visible on the Airport Moving Map, not on the 20-9 chart.

ASRSN:2229117.n: We were pushed back from gate XX and Ground gave 2 aircraft taxi instructions from the north port east on taxiway Golf. Ground then cleared us to taxi east on Golf to Mike across 9R. Gate XX requires the 2 engine taxi out due to confined spaces, I executed a 90 degree turn and was perpendicular with taxiway Golf slowly creeping on to Golf due to the jet blast restrictions. I saw Aircraft Y just leaving the north port, we had plenty of space to get in front of them, however we were not moving quickly as to not blast the gate area we were vacating. The Aircraft Y picked up speed and looked like it wasn't going to give way or even saw us so I slowed down even more. They taxied past us completely unaware we were even turning out of the gate area. There was still a gap between the Aircraft Z, I was already well past the gate departure area and approaching the dashed line on Golf. The Aircraft Z also appeared not to see us entering the taxiway, still had nose light on and was picking up speed. I turned back to the right a bit and aggressively applied the brakes as it appeared they were not stopping or giving way. As they approached I couldn't tell from my vantage point if they would strike our nose with the wingtip. On ground I said 'Aircraft Y on Golf STOP'. They proceeded past us with maybe a foot to foot and half clearance. Once we were able to get moving again we taxied down Golf and followed our instructions to 9C/FF.
ASRSN:2229117.s: The pilot reported a near collision while taxiing from Gate XX onto Taxiway Golf, where Aircraft Y and Z failed to yield despite the pilot's slow exit due to jet blast restrictions. The pilot applied aggressive brakes and issued a radio warning, resulting in a clearance of only one to one-and-a-half feet as the other aircraft passed.

ASRSN:2229118.n: On Day 0, I reported as the FO for Flight XXXX ZZZZ-ZZZ and began the preflight setup. I was the first one on the flight deck and began running through the initial preflight procedure by obtaining permission to start the APU from operations to cool down the aircraft. The setup was busy with a new departure clearance needing to be obtained with clearance delivery, and we were provided with the wrong flight plan by operations. This led to confusion with the fuel load and added workload for the crew. I mistakenly believed that checking the circuit breakers was a Relief Pilot function because the Relief Pilot completes parts of the preflight procedure such as the security and emergency equipment inspection. As a result, I failed to notice that there were circuit breakers popped on the lower panel behind the FO's seat.As we were pushing back, the CA and I noticed that neither of the iPad chargers were working, which prompted me to check the circuit breakers to see if one had popped. When I looked down at the panel to my right, I discovered that multiple circuit breakers popped. By this time, the tow crew was disconnecting. The CA instructed the Relief Pilot to contact dispatch and patch in maintenance, while I coordinated a return to the gate with ground and operations. The CA then directed me to start both engines in order to taxi back to the gate. Once we were at the gate, maintenance personnel boarded the aircraft and investigated the issue. They found that maintenance had been performed on the right pack the previous night, and the breakers had been pulled during those checks but not reset afterward. Maintenance reset the breakers and reissued a Maintenance Release. After a short delay, the flight was able to depart about 30 minutes late.
ASRSN:2229118.s: The First Officer failed to check circuit breakers during preflight, missing popped breakers caused by unreset maintenance on the right pack. This resulted in a pushback stop, return to the gate, and a 30-minute delay after maintenance reset the breakers.

ASRSN:2229121.n: Into DEN we were vectored off the arrival for spacing. At 9000ft the clearance given was direct FRONZ for the visual 35R. After some miles ATC cleared us for the visual. VNAV was disengaged at the time and so we set 7000 for FRONZ, vertical speed was engage for a gradual descent. We followed a similar vertical path to the aircraft ahead of us. ATC gave us an Altitude alert, said we were below their minimum vectoring altitude of 7500ft. I responded with we will climb to 8000ft. PF initiated a climb to which we met the glideslope profile, then LOC/GS capture within the next mile. No EGPWS (Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System)/Aural alerts came from the aircraft and a stabilized approach and normal landing followed. On STAR we were given delay vectors and slow. At 9000', vectored towards RUNWAY 35R for the visual approach. We were given visual approach to RUNWAY 35R and per ATC to proceed direct FRONZ cleared visual. We had preceding traffic in sight 5NM ahead of us and followed their similar path. I had Pilot monitoring set 7000' in the MCP (Mode Control Panel) and I started a gradual decent with AP (Autopilot) on, VS of 700'-800' FPM direct FRONZ. Within 10NM of the field (inside of DRUMM) I was at 7500' descending. At 7100' ATC notified us of a low altitude alert. We initiated a climb up to 8000' and he stated his minimum vectoring altitude in that area was 7500'. The entire time I had obstacle clearance between my aircraft and the runway. We did not receive any EGPWS (Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System) or terrain ND (Navigation Display) alerts. In fact, both navigation displays were on terrain and we showed no concerns. More importantly, I was visual and maintained clearance at all times. By the time I approached 8000' I started my decent back down to catch the glide slope on the ILS35R (backup). I complied with all stabilized approach criteria and landed uneventful on RUNWAY 35R.
ASRSN:2229121.s: The flight crew descended below the 7500ft minimum vectoring altitude while following preceding traffic on a visual approach to Denver Runway 35R. After an ATC altitude alert, they climbed to 8000ft, intercepted the ILS glide slope, and completed a stabilized landing with no terrain alerts.

ASRSN:2229132.n: During push back from Gate XX at ZZZ the push crew brought the aircraft to a stop, but no command to set brakes was given. After about 10 seconds with no aircraft movement I sensed that the ground crew failed to have me set the brakes. I then queried them twice, could hear them talking in the background, but they didn't respond. I sensed a forward rolling motion and stepped on the brakes. As I did, the ground crew gave the, set brakes" command in an excited tone. I believe we rolled forward less than a foot. I queried the ground crew if any impact with equipment or personnel occurred. They said that no such event occurred. I debriefed the ground crew and they apologized."
ASRSN:2229132.s: During pushback at ZZZ, the pilot sensed the aircraft rolling forward after the ground crew failed to command brake setting. The pilot applied brakes, stopping the aircraft after it moved less than a foot, with no impact to equipment or personnel reported.

ASRSN:2229154.n: The Left Main Bus Failed. We Detected do to the CAS (Crew Alert System) message, the disengagement of the Autopilot, and the Left Primary Flight Display (PFD) going black. Cause: LEFT Main Bus Failed. We completed and complied with the emergency procedure checklist and diverted to ZZZ. Failure of left main bus. CAS (Crew Alert System) message and Autopilot disengage left Primary Flight Display (PFD) blank.Followed check list diverted to ZZZ.
ASRSN:2229154.s: The crew experienced a left main bus failure during flight, indicated by a CAS message, autopilot disengagement, and a blank left PFD. They followed the emergency checklist and diverted to ZZZ.

ASRSN:2229156.n: L1 door slide deployed after parking at ZZZ. It was a long day/night. I verbalized my actions, but did not wait for confirmation. Fatigued, complacent and admittedly non-SOP. Very dumb mistake. I directed we complete the remaining doors disarming procedure without incident. Made the immediate contact to dispatch and operational control followed by call to my Chief Pilot. I had better review and review again company procedures for closing, arming and disarming the doors using what I believe to be very adequate procedures when applied and followed correctly. Not to add or pile on further to these procedures. Regarding fatigue possibly being a contributing factor, admit it to ones self and double the CRM enlisting backup and 3x checking. Always easy to say after the fact of course.
ASRSN:2229156.s: The flight crew deployed the L1 door slide after parking at ZZZ due to fatigue, complacency, and non-SOP actions where the reporter verbalized but did not wait for confirmation. The remaining doors were disarmed without incident, and the incident was reported to dispatch and the Chief Pilot.

ASRSN:2229160.n: Leaving SNA we were given a climb via the PIGGN 3 Runway 20R for our clearance. During our taxi for departure we were placed behind a 757 for sequence. The Captain and I talked about the possible wake turbulence and what we should do to avoid it. 757 took off and was followed by a 737, then us 2 minutes. Right after the takeoff around flap retraction altitude we hit a bit of the 757 wake. My Captain told me to pitch up to out-climb the 757 to avoid its wake. I pitched up around 12 degrees to climb as quickly as possible but in doing so we busted the at or below of 5000 at STREL. We were around 1 minute out from the fix and around 6500 feet when I noticed I climbed past it. I immediately corrected the climb and when we had switched to Departure frequency the Captain mentioned our error and our correcting actions. A major factor that caused this deviation I believe was the wake turbulence of the 757. I've been hit with wake turbulence in small GA aircraft and tossed around because of it. Once we got hit with a slight bit of wake, I wanted to climb and avoid a situation where it banked us harder than 45 degrees and being close to the ground. With the wake being lower to the ground I did not use autopilot initially. Minor factors were we had a very early show due to initially being on standby. I did not get to eat breakfast due to the early start time and we had a 1-hour ride from ZZZ to SNA. The passenger arrived early, forcing us to rush a bit to get the aircraft ready and have their bags loaded. The things we could have done better to avoid this mistake from happening are, during our dual verification, we could have reviewed the departure procedure better to emphasize the altitude restriction. After the bump from the wake I could have used the autopilot/VNAV after leveling the wings to ensure compliance with altitudes. We had an altitude deviation situation on a SID. We were cleared via the PIGGN3 Departure out of SNA which has a crossing restriction at STREL of at or below 5000 feet. We failed to level off at 5000 and were alerted by ATC of our error. We descended to 5000 and resumed the rest of the SID/flight without any further issue. There was no conflict with other aircraft. ATC did not have any further concerns. We performed our briefs to include route, altitude, squawk and frequencies. Somehow or another we both overlooked the restriction on the SID. This is rare for two pilots to miss this. In addition to this, I had a XA:30 wake-up time. The airport was also closed to traffic due to noise restrictions that are lifted at XE:00. We taxied out along with at least another 10 or more airliners to wait for the XE:00 time. We were sequenced behind a 757 and a great topic of our discussion involved how to avoid their wake turbulence. It was agreed that the steepest possible climb rate would be the best way to avoid any wake from departing airliners, especially the 757 ahead of us. I think we got trapped into focusing so much on wake avoidance that it actually drew our attention away from the SID limitations. We should have done a more thorough SID review and incorporated that into our wake avoidance attempts. Flying the line sometimes teaches us some humbling experiences. More prudence will be exercised going forward. I have to slow the pace down.
ASRSN:2229160.s: Pilots departing SNA on the PIGGN3 departure exceeded the 5000-foot restriction at STREL while aggressively climbing to avoid 757 wake turbulence. The crew corrected the altitude deviation after ATC notification, attributing the error to distraction from wake avoidance and an overlooked SID review.

ASRSN:2229193.n: During cruise we had a Eng 2 hydraulic pump low pressure light. We executed the QRH procedure and continued. About 20 minutes later we lost all hydraulic fluid and pressure on the Hydraulic B side. We executed the QRH procedure up until the deferred items. We tried coordinating with Dispatch but both ACARS and the crew phone were boot working. We were finally able to patch a phone call through a FSS where we spoke with our Dispatcher and informed them of what we had. We came up with the plan to continue to ZZZ and [notify ATC] in order to get priority handling and extended vectors on the longest runway. We coordinated with Approach and informed them we would be exiting the runway upon landing and would like emergency services to look over the plane before we taxied to the gate. We had an uneventful landing and exiting the runway. The firetrucks informed us that our #2 engine was heavily leaking a fluid and recommended we shut that engine down. We shut the engine down and after they confirmed that the leak stopped we taxied to our gate and had them follow us. We arrived at the gate with no issues.Cause: The plane had come out of the hanger in ZZZ1 and hydraulic B had a RF which we had Maintenance come out and refill. This probably should have been investigated further by Maintenance since it had just come out of maintenance servicing.
ASRSN:2229193.s: The crew experienced a total loss of Hydraulic B pressure during cruise, likely caused by an unresolved leak from recent maintenance at ZZZ1. After landing at ZZZ, fire services identified a heavy leak from Engine 2, prompting the crew to shut it down before taxiing to the gate.

ASRSN:2229223.n: While on approach to 4L, we encountered wake turbulence from a heavy on approach on 4R. We were approximately 1500 feet with the autopilot on when we started to bank to the right. I realized that this was not a correction to the localizer, so I disconnected the autopilot to bank to the left. I went full left aileron and had no control. At this point I added power and put the nose down. I continued to try and add left aileron. I was able to correct the aircraft back to the left to straight and level. We were still on glideslope and on the localizer so we continued to landing. We were visual so I asked for slight left deviation of the localizer to ensure no more wake was encountered.Cause: Encountered wake turbulence while on approach to 4L. Winds were 100 at 17 gusting to 27. As a result, the wind blew wake turbulence from a heavy just ahead of us on approach for 4R towards our final approach course.I should've known that with the winds the approach from the 4R approach might blow into the 4L path. When the event occurred, I was looking outside and could see the turbulence/wake from the heavy.
ASRSN:2229223.s: Pilots on approach to runway 4L encountered wake turbulence from a heavy aircraft on runway 4R, driven by crosswinds gusting to 27 knots. The aircraft banked right uncontrollably until the pilot disconnected the autopilot, applied power, and corrected to straight and level, allowing a continued visual landing.

ASRSN:2229231.n: This was an OE flight and my first leg as pilot flying (PF) in the left seat the Line Check Pilot (LCP) was pilot monitoring (PM) and handling radio calls, making frequent position reports. ZZZ was overloaded with traffic. There were multiple GA aircraft and helicopters all trying to use the field. After taking an extended vector to allow other traffic in, we were given an approach clearance for Runway XX. The winds were a direct crosswind gusting to 25 kts. We had planned to roll to the end to spare the brakes any excess heat so we could make the turn as quick as possible. While rolling to the end, I had noticed there was a taildragging aircraft sitting there so we had nowhere to go. We were stopped on the runway waiting for him to move out of the way, and in our minds this would have entailed taxiing to the departure end in use (XX) and instead this individual proceeded to taxi onto the runway (XY) without making any radio calls and hugging the end of the pavement to make room. During this process, I heard another aircraft getting ready to takeoff of Runway XX while we were still holding for the small aircraft to clear. Over the radio we announced we were still on the runway. At this point there may have been three aircraft on the runway but this is speculation. Once able to taxi onto the taxiway and clear the runway, the LCP said 'why dont you use Runway XX so its easier on all of us' which was met with the response: 'what are you an air traffic controller?'. This individual also mentioned something about a maintenance run up or flight. We tried to get a tail number but at this point we were unable. I then hear the aircraft on the departure end on XX announce their takeoff. This means they either had to takeoff over this individual or if he decided to takeoff without announcing it, potentially had a near miss event. After this we taxi to the gate, shutdown and deplane. It is our agreed opinions this individual compromised the safety of multiple aircraft and lives with irresponsible airmanship and a dangerous attitude. Cause: Dangerous and unprofessional airman.
ASRSN:2229231.s: A pilot flying an OE flight reported a runway incursion at ZZZ where a taildragging aircraft entered Runway XY without radio contact while the crew held on Runway XX. The reporter attributed the safety compromise to the other pilot's dangerous and unprofessional airmanship.

ASRSN:2229233.n: Aircraft X Ferry Flight. I WAS PM. We were cleared visual for XX and we backed it up with the VOR Z XX. We received a Terrain warning while were we turning for final and maintain visual separation. We were 600 - 800 Ft above Terrain. Continued for a Normal landing. Cause: Complacency. And seeing the Terrain. Talking about it. And we still got a Caution GPWS. Suggestions: Turn in before the terrain. Maintain more altitude before descent for visual here at ZZZZ
ASRSN:2229233.s: The Pilot Monitoring on Aircraft X received a GPWS caution while turning for final at 600–800 feet above terrain during a visual approach. The crew attributed the warning to complacency and discussion of the terrain but completed a normal landing.

ASRSN:2229267.n: During climb from ZZZZ, en route to ZZZZ1, CA's PFD (Primary Flight Display) began displaying SPD LIM flag and no vertical flight director guidance along with upper/lower speed limit bars moving up and down along speed tape intermittently. Vertical Flight Director guidance bars became intermittent during climb, alternating between SPD LIM present and vertical guidance. Referenced FM (Flight Manual) and found only reference to SPD LIM flag associated to the 737 MAX Equipment Cooling off and among the list of indicators for Airspeed Unreliable. All airspeed/altitude raw data matched across all indicators.Contacted dispatch and Maintenance Control for further guidance. As we were discussing no operator procedures that could clear the issue, the CA's control column stick shaker activated momentarily, while all raw data across all displays showed normal operations. We elected to return to ZZZZ, were cleared by Maintenance Control guidance for an overweight landing. During descent Auto Slat Fail light also illuminated. Returned to ZZZZ uneventfully.
ASRSN:2229267.s: During climb from ZZZZ, the Captain's PFD displayed SPD LIM flags and intermittent flight director guidance, followed by a momentary stick shaker activation and Auto Slat Fail light. The crew returned to ZZZZ for an overweight landing after Maintenance Control confirmed no operator procedures could clear the anomalies.

ASRSN:2229269.n: I was PF, Cap was PM, normal T/O until PM standard 100 kts callout, at that time I noticed the master caution light on and I ask what is it?" PM responds "door light ON" immediately I ask, reject?" Half a second after that the cap announced "I have the aircraft, rejecting" after that CA took control of the aircraft and executed a normal RTO (Rejected Take-Off) procedure at about 105 KTS. After slow down the aircraft I called TWR to inform about the RTO, ATC asked for the reason and if we needed any assistance, and I responded, reason was the door light on and we didn't need any assistance. We cleared the runway, performed RTO checklist, after landing flow, and started making coordinations with operations and maintenance for a gate and inspections. After parking at the gate a post flight inspection by MX (Maintenance) determined one tire needed to be replaced for excessive wear."
ASRSN:2229269.s: The Pilot Flying rejected takeoff at 105 knots after the Pilot Monitoring reported a door light illumination. Maintenance later found one tire required replacement due to excessive wear from the rejected takeoff.

ASRSN:2229405.n: Before starting the descent for ZZZ, current weather and NOTAMS were obtained for ZZZ. PF briefed an approach for LOC RWY XX. The glide slope was out of service. MDA was set for 1700 according to GS OUT Minimums on the approach plate. The descent was started momentarily after. We were vectored to intercept the localizer. The PF switched to green needles" to intercept the course. The autopilot had a hard time maintaining a straight course, and it kept swaying side to side. The aircraft was configured fully and the "Before Landing" checklist was completed. A Missed Approach altitude of 3000 was set. Before reaching the FAF, the PM read out a Groundspeed of 173 and told the PF he needed a descent rate of about 800 to 900 FPM to descend to landing. At 0.2 miles from FAF, the PF started a descent of 900 FPM. Upon reaching minimums, the PM called out "Missed Approach;" but the PF thought he saw lights and continued. Shortly after, the crew broke out and saw a VASI that indicated 4 Red Lights as well as a banking attitude. Shortly thereafter, the GLIDESLOPE EGPWS (Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System) aural alert sounded, and the PF initiated a Go-Around. At the same time, Tower said they saw the aircraft breaking out and said they were low. Tower then instructed the crew to Go-Around. The crew was already going around. The crew performed a Go-Around, and Tower instructed them to climb and maintain 3000. The crew then contacted Departure to receive further instructions for a second approach. The PF briefed the same approach but was going to stay in "White Needles" this time to intercept the course. The autopilot did a better job maintaining a straight course. The crew performed all the pertinent checklists. The crew executed the approach again and broke out at minimums. The aircraft landed without further incident and taxied to parking. The crew then debriefed the flight.The PF should have executed a Missed Approach when the PM called out "Missed Approach." This, along with an autopilot that was not maintaining a straight course, contributed to an unstable approach. We brief these things for a reason, and as pilots carrying passengers we need to always keep safety first. If the runway is not in sight, then go-around. It's simple as that." Shooting LOC XX into ZZZ we hit minimums. Upon reaching minimums I stated 'missed approach' verbally to which it was not executed. PF continued through minimums and declared 'runway in sight, landing' at which point we received, of what I thought was, an aural 'TOO LOW' warning and then were told by Tower, 'Aircraft X you're looking low, go around' to which we executed a missed approach procedure.Cause: PF fixating outside instead of inside, PM not stating missed approach a second time.Suggestions: As PF keep eyes inside and rely on PM to declare deviations/ visual cues.
ASRSN:2229405.s: The Pilot Flying continued a LOC approach at ZZZ past minimums despite the Pilot Monitoring's callout, causing an EGPWS alert and ATC go-around instruction due to an unstable approach. The crew executed a missed approach, corrected the autopilot mode, and landed safely on a second attempt.

ASRSN:2229450.n: CHSRunway 15 landing rolloutDuring landing rollout on runway 15, I noticed an aircraft similar to an Aircraft Y making a takeoff roll on runway 21. As the flying pilot I transmitted on tower frequency What is this?". Tower immediately issued a hold short runway 21 to us. We were fortunate to be slow enough to comply. The other aircraft on runway 21 took off. We continued and taxied to the gate without further incident. The tower controller did say that he intended to issue and land runway 15 and hold short runway 21 which we would not have been able to accept. The ATIS stated LAHSO for GA only. As we did nothing wrong I am submitting this report as this is a serious matter and needs to be addressed."
ASRSN:2229450.s: The pilot reported a runway incursion risk during landing rollout on Runway 15 at CHS when another aircraft began takeoff on Runway 21. The tower issued a hold short clearance that the pilot complied with, noting the controller's intended clearance was unsafe and the ATIS incorrectly stated LAHSO applied only to general aviation.

ASRSN:2229617.n: I was sitting left seat while my CFI was flying right seat getting currency in the BE-55. WE had done one full stop landing and taxi back previously and were doing another (he needed three for currency) and as we were landing this time for a touch and go, he asked me to get the flaps and I inadvertently raised the gear which result in a dual prop strike, etc.
ASRSN:2229617.s: The pilot in the left seat inadvertently raised the landing gear while the CFI flew a touch-and-go in a BE-55. This error caused a dual propeller strike during the landing phase.

ASRSN:2229638.n: We were doing pattern work on 21 at TTA. One other traffic was ahead of us when we entered. On the second lap, Aircraft Y attempted to enter the RWY, assuming he was trying to take off from A3, but stopped just before any part of his plane would cross onto the RWY. A decision was made to lift off and climb on upwind before we would cross taxiway A3 as a precaution. He proceeded to back taxi on active runway to taxiway A4 and idled there for a long time, before taxing on A in the direction of RWY3's departure end while Aircraft Z was taxing to 21 on the same taxiway, in the opposite direction (to the runway the traffics were all using). No radio calls were heard from Aircraft YWe returned to ZZZ eventually and no more safety incidents occurred
ASRSN:2229638.s: During pattern work at TTA, Aircraft Y entered the active runway without radio communication, prompting the reporting pilot to climb early as a precaution. Aircraft Y subsequently back-taxied and idled on the runway before moving toward the departure end while Aircraft Z approached from the opposite direction.

ASRSN:2229639.n: Caution Obstacle EGPWS (Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System) call. We were inbound to ZZZ on the RNAV XX. We had to go missed twice.I set the minimums 100ft above the published LNAV mins since I'm a green captain.On our second approach we were approximately 3NM from the MAP (Missed Approach Point) and we hit a gust and had a momentary pitch up and then pitch down. The aircraft gave a 'CAUTION OBSTACLE' call and then the tower came on and told us to check altitude we were above MDA which was 1440 and we were at 1600.
ASRSN:2229639.s: The green captain flying an RNAV approach to ZZZ triggered a false EGPWS "Caution Obstacle" call during a gust-induced pitch change. Although the aircraft was at 1600 feet, well above the 1440-foot MDA, the tower instructed an altitude check after the crew executed two missed approaches.

ASRSN:2229667.n: I was returning to LDJ on an IFR flight plan due to rapidly deteriorating weather. While LDJ was still reporting VFR, as was EWR and surrounding airports, there was weather in between my departure airport ZZZ and LDJ.I opted for the GPS-A approach into Linden, the only available instrument approach at the airport. The controller had to issue numerous delay vectors due to traffic conflicts to the Runway 04 approach at EWR. I was eventually cleared for the approach at DAPVY but warned that I would have to cut off the approach in approximately 7 miles.As I approached GEZSY on the GPS-A approach at 1400 feet, I still could not see the airport. Wanting to get down below a cloud deck in front of me, I asked for the visual approach. However, without the airport in sight, ATC could not clear me as I was below the MVA.A second controller came on the radio as I approached GEZSY (just 5 miles from the point where I was told I had approximately 7 miles before needing to terminate the approach) saying that I needed to either have the airport in sight or terminate the approach and hold.At this point I requested to cancel IFR as I could see that it would be VFR at my destination and there was ample cloud clearance for me to get down before arriving at LDJ. However, I do not feel it was appropriate for ATC to apply this level of pressure as I was flying single pilot IFR on a published approach.After I cancelled IFR, another pilot on frequency made a comment to ATC thanking them for being patient (presumably with me.) This was not an appropriate comment for a pilot to make on frequency.It is unsafe for ATC to pressure pilots to make decisions like this in IMC, especially single pilot. I am very familiar with the area and was comfortable continuing VFR. However, someone unfamiliar with the area could get into a lot of trouble very quickly.This has been a persistent issue with N90 and the GPS-A approach. N90 is always very hesitant to allow a pilot to fly the GPS-A approach. If they do not want us flying this approach, it should be removed. If there are non-standard procedures they want us to follow, they need to be published.A few years ago there was a fatal crash on the GPS-A approach at BAUTZ. The approach is very difficult to fly - and the fatal crash involved a pilot who is familiar with the area. ATC and the FAA need to take steps to improve the instrument approach to Linden, or remove it entirely.
ASRSN:2229667.s: A single-pilot IFR flight to LDJ on the GPS-A approach was pressured by ATC to terminate due to traffic and visibility issues, leading the pilot to cancel IFR and continue VFR. The reporter attributes the incident to ATC pressure and the difficulty of the approach, citing a past fatal crash and calling for the procedure's removal or improvement.

ASRSN:2229671.n: While starting the aircraft, the throttle was advanced too much and on engine start, the plane moved forward entering the south taxiway. No other aircraft or ground vehicles were in the vicinity. I contact ground and was cleared to taxi.My lack of currency lead to the throttle being advanced too far for engine start and, with the primed engine, the quick start led to a momentary loss of controls.Fortunately, no other aircraft or ground vehicles were in the vicinity.
ASRSN:2229671.s: The pilot advanced the throttle too far during engine start, causing the aircraft to move forward onto the south taxiway. This incident resulted from a lack of currency and a quick start with a primed engine, leading to a momentary loss of control, though no other traffic was present.

ASRSN:2229672.n: Bird strike on left downwind RWY XX due to which windshield broke. Immediate landing was performed. No injuries and emergency was not declared. Bird strike on left downwind runway XX. Due to that windshield broke. And did a immediate landing. No injuries and emergency was not declared.
ASRSN:2229672.s: The crew experienced a bird strike on the left downwind for Runway XX, which broke the windshield. They performed an immediate landing with no injuries and did not declare an emergency.

ASRSN:2229673.n: We conducted a visual approach to ZZZ runway XX, which all other traffic were using. We made numerous calls on CTAF throughout our descent and approach. On final approach, a small aircraft cut in front of us and landed on XX. We still had sufficient room to land behind it, and so we continued. However, as we were watching to verify it had cleared the runway, another small aircraft immediately landed on opposite end of our runway, which was runway XY and not XX, the active runway. This aircraft had made no radio calls and was attempting to get in before we landed. Also Because of the slope of the runway, we were unable to see this aircraft. We landed normally and as we taxied in, we then saw them clearing our runway. In their haste to get away, they hurriedly taxied to runway XX and took off. Our company aircraft was waiting for us to land so they could depart IFR and they were holding short of runway XX and could have witnessed the event.
ASRSN:2229673.s: The pilot reported a visual approach to runway XX where a small aircraft landed without radio calls on the opposite end of the active runway, obscured by slope. The intruder hurriedly taxied to runway XX and took off while the reporting aircraft landed normally behind another traffic.

ASRSN:2229681.n: I began my preflight, engine cowling inspection, along with all calculations needed prior to my flight. I began to taxi to runway XX. The winds were at 050 and 10 kts when I listened before taking off. I never heard the station broadcast system say the gust factor prior to or while in flight. I then began my take off and climbed up to pattern altitude. A PC-12 was coming in on a 8 mile base leg from the south for runway XY. I made my crosswind pattern leg and departed to the south maintained visual separation and let the PC-12 know I was not a factor. I then waited until they landed and said clear of the runway XY to begin a re-entry to the pattern on the downwind leg for runway XY via a 45° entry. I then did all procedures in the pattern needed, and came in for a touch and go on runway XY. Had no issues on approach, landing or takeoff, I then did another lap in the pattern following all procedures needed. Once I was on final my approach was stable I hit a pocket of very slight turbulence but maintained a stable approach. I then landed, did all procedures to begin takeoff and then began to rotate, after reaching rotation speed. At lift off I felt either turbulence or a gust of wind dictate the plane causing the plane to dance around and since I was low to the ground I tried to not let the plane get off course or any unusual attitude. Then once I was at a safe altitude in the pattern, Aircraft Y had told me the winds changed and were now favoring runway XZ. I then departed the traffic pattern again on the crosswind leg to the south and listened in to the weather station. Which did state the winds were at 330. So I waited for Aircraft Y to depart from the pattern and began to rejoin the traffic pattern again on the downwind leg at a 45° entry but for runway XZ. I did all of the procedures needed for the pattern. Once I was on final, I had a stable approach and landed safely on XZ and began to taxi back to parking. I then checked the tanks for remaining fuel and oil levels after engine shut off the aircraft parked and tied down. I did not notice any damage to the aircraft while checking the tanks or engine.
ASRSN:2229681.s: The pilot conducted touch-and-go operations at an uncontrolled field, experiencing a gust-induced aircraft attitude change during a low-altitude takeoff on runway XY. The pilot maintained control, switched to runway XZ after wind changes were reported, and landed safely with no reported damage.

ASRSN:2229686.n: Departing ZZZ1 we were heading north, and suddenly a parachutist under canopy appeared directly in front of us, about 100 ft above. Did not have time to react and they passed safely overhead. We then observed the jump plane well below descending in a spiral to the airport.No flight following advisories from ZZZ ATC were avaliable, but we were monitoring the local approach frequency. No jumpers away notification was heard on frequency. The local airport does not publish a ctaf or Unicom.Was surprised given the local traffic volume for the event that the jump area was active. This was a flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2. We were climbing out from a ZZZ departure. Upon initial departure from ZZZ, we stayed under the ZZZ3 bravo, below 3000 feet. Upon clearing the ZZZ3 bravo, we climbed to an eventual altitude of 9500. Upon passing through somewhere around 3000 or 3200 feet (in the vicinity of the east side of ZZZ1) we saw a parachute jumper above and to the left of the plane. I immediately turned to the right. We were in the Parachute Jump Area (PJA) that is around ZZZ. We had VFR flight following established and were in communication with ATC. I do not recall which ATC facility I called and established flight following with. Prior to departure, I did a complete flight briefing, and saw no mention of active parachute jumping. We were also not advised by ATC of any parachute activity, and had no way to know if the PJA was active. We were not monitoring UNICOM for ZZZ, and did not think to. While I believe we were within approximately 500 to 1000 feet vertically and laterally from the jumper, I believe the trajectory of the plane and position of the jumper was such that there was not imminent risk of interception. The incident was certainly unnerving and alarming. I believe that if either the PJA being active has been in a NOTAM, or if I had been advised by ATC, the matter could have been avoided.
ASRSN:2229686.s: A pilot departing ZZZ1 on a VFR flight following to ZZZ2 encountered a parachutist at approximately 3,000 feet within an active Parachute Jump Area. The pilot executed an evasive turn after receiving no prior advisories from ATC or NOTAMs regarding the jump activity.

ASRSN:2229692.n: I was conducting a flight review in Aircraft X. I was on a right downwind turning right base for Runway XX at ZZZ in trail of a CE-152, Aircraft Y. Aircraft Z was making a left hand pattern for Runway XX, even after being advised that Runway XX is right hand pattern at ZZZ. Due to this flagrant disregard of 91.126, they nearly collided with Aircraft Y. I witnessed Aircraft Y make a sharp turn at a high bank angle to avoid a collision. The entire time, Aircraft Z was clogging the frequency with meowing, whispered tail numbers, excessive chatter and other generally poor radio discipline despite there being 4 airplanes in the traffic pattern. Despite this mid-air, on a subsequent lap in the pattern, they turned an early right crosswind and created a collision hazard with my aircraft. I witnessed them make a sharp left turn at a high bank angle to avoid a conflict. Again, despite nearly two mid-airs in the space of about 15 minutes, the pilots continued their unprofessional radio calls.
ASRSN:2229692.s: During a flight review at ZZZ, the pilot observed Aircraft Z violating right-hand pattern rules and poor radio discipline, causing two near mid-air collisions with Aircraft Y and the reporter's aircraft. Aircraft Z forced both other pilots to execute sharp, high-bank turns to avoid conflict.

ASRSN:2229701.n: While concentrating on maintaining separation with other aircraft in the area, I neglected to maintain minimum 1,000 altitude as I passed over a populated area while the terrain was also rising.
ASRSN:2229701.s: An air traffic controller failed to maintain the required 1,000-foot minimum altitude over a populated area with rising terrain while concentrating on aircraft separation. The controller reported this altitude violation as a result of neglecting terrain awareness during the separation task.

ASRSN:2229706.n: At the end of a 3.5 flight with turbulence I Mistakenly Landed downwind. The landing was in the center of the runway but heavy braking was required. My right foot didn't find the brake pedal so I veered off the runway to the left and hit a runway distance sign with the left wing tip. The plane stopped about 50 feet further. The field was deserted but eventually two men came and we pushed the plane back to the runway where I started the engine and taxied to parking.Upon inspection the next day the only damage was a small dent in the wing so since I have a repairman certificate I decided the plane was airworthy and flew it home to ZZZ1.While in ZZZ I called the numbers at the airport and reached the police department and reported the mishap. I will call airport manager and arrange to pay for the damage.
ASRSN:2229706.s: The pilot mistakenly landed downwind after a turbulent flight, veered off the runway due to missed braking, and struck a distance sign with the left wingtip. The pilot declared the aircraft airworthy after inspecting a small dent and flew it home, subsequently reporting the incident to the police.

ASRSN:2229712.n: Cleared for RNAV XX (winds XXX/10). I was using recently installed Autothrottles w/ Autopilot (AP) engaged. Past FAF, at approximately 1700', ATC cancelled clearance, instructed me to maintain 2,000 heading (HDG) 320. I failed to clean up plane (retract flaps) while turning to 320 and trying to climb back to 2,000. As I added power to climb back to 2,000, plane pitched up aggressively to avoid overspeed, as ldg flap max speed is 160kts. Poor airmanship on my part. I am heading for annual recurrent this week , and will be vigorously practicing missed approach/go around procedures.
ASRSN:2229712.s: The pilot, flying an aircraft with autothrottles and autopilot engaged during an RNAV approach, failed to retract flaps after ATC cancelled the clearance and instructed a climb to 2,000 feet. This resulted in an aggressive pitch-up to avoid overspeed, which the pilot attributed to poor airmanship.

ASRSN:2229714.n: Taxiing to Runway 19 from the FBO, I had difficulty finding the threshold and might have crossed over it (but not quite on the runway itself) while waiting for clearance to take off.As there were ATC delays (I had filed quite recently before attempting to depart and there was an incoming plane on an instrument flight plan at this non-towered airport), I decided to play it safe and taxi back to well back from the runway.It's possible this wasn't an official taxiway as it had no designation on the taxi diagram (no letter assigned that I could see), but this day, as years before when we diverted to it, I've seen it used fairly frequently. In fact when it was time to retry ATC and depart, a jet announced it was taxiing to the same runway from the FBO and headed down the same path I had used. (So, rather than wait to call ATC and get clearance, I departed VFR promptly and picked up my clearance in the air, as I was likely to delay the jet by waiting for ATC to clear me to depart.)It would seem wise, at this airport, to officially designate the taxiways as needed, including proper and clearly visible thresholds. In general this airport seems to need some tender love and care, it wasn't in as good shape as I recall from years ago, but with three runways in its location would seem to be worth keeping going.
ASRSN:2229714.s: A pilot taxiing to Runway 19 at a non-towered airport struggled to locate the threshold and potentially crossed it while waiting for clearance. The pilot returned to a safe position, later departing VFR to avoid delaying an arriving jet, and recommended officially designating taxiways and marking thresholds.

ASRSN:2229715.n: Upon departing RWY XX out of ZZZ passing 1000-1100AGL, I had a Electronic Flight Instrument System (EFIS) Failure causing complete loss of my Primary Flight Display (PFD) and Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI). Both screens went blank. Conditions were VMC on departure. I switched to standby instruments once I had a complete EFIS failure. Tower provided assistance to me to make initial turn to heading 273 as I was working the avionics failure. I was switched to departure controller as I was flying the SID (ZZZZZ1.ZZZZZ) off standby instruments. I was able to accomplish the emergency/abnormal checklist for a EFIS FAILURE which required resetting the flight guidance computer circuit breaker. I informed departure controller that I lost my PFD and HSI displays and that I was running the abnormal checklist. I requested to stay direct ZZZZZ until I got both screens recovered and the autopilot engaged because I was single pilot. I informed the departure controller that I was able to reset the system and the controller cleared me direct ZZZZZ2. The departure controller gave me a number to contact upon landing. I called the number and explained what happened to a Tower controller.
ASRSN:2229715.s: A single-pilot aircraft experienced a complete EFIS failure with blank PFD and HSI screens while departing RWY XX at 1000-1100 AGL in VMC. The pilot used standby instruments, reset the flight guidance computer circuit breaker, and was cleared direct ZZZZZ2 after recovering the displays.

ASRSN:2229731.n: While we were in the run up area performing normal checks, we had the right engine catch on fire. We were parked in an area with no other aircraft around with the engines running with the aircraft not in motion. We were able to do normal magneto checks but then lost sensors to the right engine and then we looked out the right side to notice that the right engine had caught on fire. We had 3 people on board. We cut the mixtures to both engines immediately and exited out the main door. Ramp people nearby came running with a large fire extinguisher and put the fire out. At this time we are not sure of what caused the fire. Nothing else was damaged.The local airport called the local fire department. They arrived on scene about 10 minutes after the fire was put out. We gave verbal statements about the event and gave them our names, phone numbers, and address in case of further contact required. We towed and secured the plane after fire officials said it was safe to move.
ASRSN:2229731.s: Three occupants in a stationary aircraft experienced a right engine fire during run-up checks after losing engine sensors. Ramp personnel extinguished the fire with a large extinguisher, and the cause remains unknown with no other damage reported.

ASRSN:2229739.n: Myself, a VO, and a Driver of a chase vehicle were conducting C-UAS Radar testing for our employer in the city of Location A to refine our detection of UAS. We were operating under part 107, as a commercial operation. We had issued and received our LAANC authorization through Aloft.ai, as we do for all of our testing. Our flight path was north and south along Location B in Location A. Our Authorization was up to 400'AGL from the southern end of our approved corridor to the North-Western edge of the Class D. I was in the Backseat of the vehicle as the R-PIC, my visual observer was in the front passenger seat, and our driver was driving the vehicle 100-150m behind the drone during our north and south runs. We were starting our run to the north from a location starting at Location C and Headed north. When the drone was at Location D Indicated by flight logs when evasive descent occurred, I heard the indistinguishable roar of an F-16 as it flew fast and very low over our chase vehicle, flying from the East, and turning towards the north as if they were doing their break to land maneuver, and were in the crosswind to downwind leg of the pattern. I looked out the left side window and would estimate that it was at roughly 400-600'AGL, I immediately descended the drone to around 210' AGL as an evasive maneuver to stay clear of the F16. Their altitude 3nm away from the end of RWXX at ZZZ seemed way too low for being that far out in the pattern regardless of the maneuvering they were doing. I don't think collision was imminent however, if the incident had happened about 30 seconds earlier, I believe the drone would have posed a threat to the flight safety of the F16. As a manned Commercial pilot, I would have been calling the tower about another manned aircraft being as close to an aircraft I was operating if an F-16 had gotten that close to me under manned operations. The DJI Air 3s that we are operating with has 'Airsense' which is ADSB-In and will alert the operator via the controller/GS when an aircraft is present in the area and may pose a potential collision hazard. Since the F-16's don't broadcast ADSB, I was unaware of their operations that day since I had not seen any up until that point. Normally we operate with ADSB-Exchange on a tablet to monitor other air traffic within our operating area and to try and expect oncoming traffic as it relates to ZZZ so we can mitigate potential incidents such as this. However, again because F-16's do not broadcast ADSB-Out, we did not know they were operating until it was directly overhead our chase vehicle. Even though the F-16 had flown behind and around to the front of the drone, I still descended to 'give room' to the F-16. We have access to Handheld Radios that monitor the ZZZ ATC traffic, but with the F-16's primarily communicating with UHF to the ATC tower there, I doubt that any transmission from them would have came through clear enough to understand that one was doing a break to land. As remedial action from this incident, our VO's have been re-trained on scanning the airspace around us when taking short breaks from maintaining visual contact with the drone, and have been instructed on the importance of air to air conflict resolutions techniques such as descending, stopping, ascending, etc. I take full responsibility for the safety of the flight an am a huge advocate for all of the flights conducted for myself and the company I work for. I have successfully taught a class of 10 individuals and they have all passed their Remote Pilot written tests and have received their Part 107 certificates in an effort to get more people qualified for the use of drones in our line of work. Safety is always number one and I hope some sort of resolution can come from this that may mitigate any further potential issues with air to air near misses with fast movers such as the F-16's. I am open to further discussion with the FAA, Air National Guard base, and ZZZ to work towards a collaborative solution to mitigate these happenings as the frequency of our testing will increase with time and the possibility of this occurring again may still be present.
ASRSN:2229739.s: A Part 107 drone operator, visual observer, and driver conducting C-UAS testing in Location A descended a DJI Air 3s from 400' AGL to 210' AGL after an F-16 flew low overhead. The near miss occurred because the F-16 did not broadcast ADSB, preventing the crew from detecting the aircraft until it was directly over their chase vehicle.

ASRSN:2229799.n: Two engine taxi out from gate XX at ZZZ .Route Taxiway 1 2 3 to Runway XXR. Multiple aircraft in- line for takeoff.We are probably about number 5. Waiting with parking brake set and engines at idle the fire warning happens.We both get startled by the sudden warning. I shut down the engine and press the lighted fire button on the overhead.The warning goes out. I call the cabin, they see/ hear nothing abnormal. The FO calls the tower, they send all the services.They see nothing. We then eventually return to the gate and deplane the customers. Maintenance eventually takes the plane out of service . Six and a half hours later we fly another aircraft to ZZZ1.
ASRSN:2229799.s: The crew experienced a false fire warning while taxiing with engines at idle, prompting an immediate engine shutdown and fire button activation. Ground services found no abnormality, leading to a return to the gate, passenger deplaning, and a six-and-a-half-hour delay before flying a replacement aircraft.

ASRSN:2229815.n: On left base turn to final to runway XXL ATC called out traffic below us no factor. We then got a TCAS RA telling me Don't descend. I leveled off at 4000' and the traffic showed 400 feet below us. As we were calling out the RA to ATC we got a CLIMB NOW TCAS RA with traffic showing 200 feet below us. Immediately flew the RA and climbed to 4200' when clear of conflict was announced and returned to 4000' and shot the approach. We never saw the traffic.
ASRSN:2229815.s: The pilot on left base to runway XXL received a "Don't Descend" TCAS RA with traffic 400 feet below, followed by a "Climb Now" RA with traffic 200 feet below. The crew climbed to 4,200 feet to resolve the conflict, returned to 4,000 feet, and completed the approach without visually sighting the traffic.

ASRSN:2229826.n: Push crew advised ready to push. Clearance was obtained and brakes released. Push crew then advised that a priority package was enroute and we needed to hold for it. Captain was not advised to set the parking brake but informed crew of the necessity and brakes were set. 2 packages were loaded and ramp advised ready to continue the push. After push had begun, we received a hazardous goods notification. We were not to expect hazardous goods and push crew did not advise that hazardous goods had been loaded. Dangerous Goods report was sent after 2nd brake release. Prior to push, Ground called ready for brake release. After brakes were released, they said that they needed to add a package and could not push until it was here, as directed by Ops. We were already captured, we set the parking brake and waited. Initially Ground did not want the parking brake set, but we communicated that it was set. They loaded the 'package', and we reran the before push checklist. We were re-cleared to push, during the push is when we got a DG (Dangerous Goods) final summary. We then sent the Dangerous Goods report but we were already pushed. At no time were we expecting any DGs nor was it communicated that that was the 'package' we were expecting.
ASRSN:2229826.s: The flight crew halted a pushback to load an unannounced package, which was later identified as unexpected Dangerous Goods. The crew set the parking brake during the delay and submitted a Dangerous Goods report after the push resumed, noting no prior communication regarding the hazardous nature of the cargo.

ASRSN:2229829.n: Noticed 2' crack w/ depth at cruise. Complied with QRC, notified dispatch and Maintenance control, and Diverted to ZZZ with no further issues.
ASRSN:2229829.s: The pilot noticed a 2-inch crack with depth at cruise, complied with the QRC, notified dispatch and maintenance, and diverted to ZZZ with no further issues.

ASRSN:2229834.n: To avoid the engine hitting the bridge I proceeded to raise bridge and move to get out of the engines way. Very hairy. I would say the plane was forward past the mark by 40 or 50 feet. It was on [gate] X which is a wide body bridge. I was on the correct bridge to park a 737.
ASRSN:2229834.s: The pilot reported parking a Boeing 737 at a wide-body gate, where the aircraft overshot the mark by 40 to 50 feet. To prevent the engine from striking the bridge, the pilot raised the bridge and moved the aircraft, describing the event as very hairy.

ASRSN:2229840.n: We picked up our plane and proceeded to taxiway 1. I was the driver. My move team partner handled the radio. We got the route twice from the controller. My partner read back taxiway 2/taxiway 3/taxiway 4 hold short of taxiway 5. As we entered taxiway 3, there was a plane opposite direction screaming off the runway. I stopped of course. Tower said for us to continue. We then went to taxiway 5 to hold short. After we cleared after a few minutes, we proceeded to go the rest of the way on taxiway 6. About halfway to Maintenance Control, the controller called us back to confirm taxiway 2, taxiway 3, taxiway 4, taxiway 6. My partner said affirmative. My manager clearly has info now that I was in the right that he did say taxiway 2, taxiway 3, hold short of taxiway 5. There was no mention of that aircraft or a STOP!! from the controller. We have evidence now that we were right about the route and somehow nobody saw that aircraft. He was coming off I believe runway XX left.
ASRSN:2229840.s: A ground driver and radio operator received conflicting taxi instructions from Tower while moving an aircraft, causing a stop when another aircraft exited the runway. The controller directed them to continue, and the reporter concluded the team was correct about the route despite the controller's failure to mention the conflicting aircraft or issue a stop command.

ASRSN:2229842.n: Aircraft X had called for off gate XX and was given a tail North push approved. Aircraft Y was taxing for gate XY and called as made turn South on taxiway 1 for XY. Aircraft Y was advised to give way to Aircraft X as they turned tail North. Crew continued into the ramp causing Aircraft X to stop there push.
ASRSN:2229842.s: Aircraft Y taxied onto the ramp while Aircraft X was approved for a tail North push, causing Aircraft X to stop. The incident occurred because Aircraft Y ignored instructions to give way and continued into the ramp area.

ASRSN:2229843.n: When airplane return to a position CA requested to connect air conditioner, GPU, due to make test with engine 1, driver for this flight got too close to engine 2 even when marshal was making stop signal causing an incident that was reported to his manager.
ASRSN:2229843.s: A ground driver approached too close to engine 2 while connecting ground power and air conditioning for an engine 1 test, ignoring the marshaller's stop signal. This incident was reported to the driver's manager.

ASRSN:2229862.n: Aircraft X was pushed back into Taxiway 1. Once push was commenced the push driver told the Captain to set the brakes, response was that the brakes were set. The team continued to disconnect the tow bar. At this time the flight encountered an issue and wanted to return to the gate. The aircraft's brakes were released and the aircraft rolled towards the bar and push back tug, no power emitted. The push back drivers comms lead was still connected and told the Captain to set the brakes as the team were still removing GSE (Ground Support Equipment) and the wing walk marshal was still in the taxiway producing a stop sign with the wands. The aircraft set the brakes again whilst the push team disconnected fully and made their way off of the taxiway. The marshal gave the salute and the aircraft returned to gate for Maintenance Control to troubleshoot the issue.
ASRSN:2229862.s: Aircraft X rolled toward the tug and GSE after the crew released brakes to return to the gate while the push team was still disconnecting equipment. The marshal signaled a stop, the brakes were re-applied, and the aircraft returned to the gate for maintenance troubleshooting.

ASRSN:2229907.n: We were cruise FL430, on Y436 between DIZNY and EBEAR (I think) and talking to JAX Center. We initially got a Crew Alerting System (CAS) Turn Coordinator, and a minute or so later, while my FO was reading from the Norm/Abnormal Checklist, we got mechanical malfunction on GPS2 CAS message. While my FO was reading the checklist for the mechanical malfunction message and we were discussing the issues, the plane started veering off course (to the right) and had begun a very slow descent (without any audible alerts telling us the autopilot had disconnected). The aircraft acted like it was lost... I immediately selected heading mode (the plane had begun a slow right turn off course). But, the plane did NOT respond to heading mode, so I immediately began hand-flying to get back on course (turning left) and recovering the lost altitude (roughly losing 300 feet, as I asked ATC to confirm). We alerted ATC of GPS jamming, asked for a heading on course to OGGRE (as the plane was still kind of lost). Once I got the plane under control and back to FL430, I asked ATC if there were any separation issues. He stated that there were no issues and that he advised us that he let the military know to stop doing what they were doing.
ASRSN:2229907.s: The crew of flight Y436 at FL430 experienced GPS2 failure and uncommanded deviation, which they attributed to military GPS jamming. The pilot hand-flew to recover 300 feet and course after the autopilot failed to respond, and ATC confirmed the military ceased the interference.

ASRSN:2229915.n: Started as a normal flight. I was pilot flying. It was snowing in ZZZ and on the way to the runway we got de-iced and did an ice test A with no faults. After de-ice we elected to keep the APU off since it wasn't needed and AOM rev 10 allows it. It was an icing take off with engine bleeds selected and the icing override knob set to ENG (Engine). On the climb flow after Person A set the icing override knob to AUTO we got an E2 anti ice fail message on the EICAS around 2000 msl. Person A transferred coms to me has he grabbed the QRH. After completing the QRH checklist we decided to continue to ZZZ1 because the valve failed in the open position which did not compromise the safety of the flight. Shortly after passing though 10000msl we got BLEED 2 OVERTEMP message on the EICAS. Person A grabbed the QRH again and ran the associate checklist.
